Andrew Ng calls this the module people find most valuable, and I agree with
him, but for a specific reason tied to my own work. Reflection and tool use make
an agent capable. This module makes it improvable. Without a disciplined way to
measure and diagnose failures, you are guessing at what to fix next, and
guessing does not scale once your pipeline has five or six chained components,
which mine does.

## Jargon, explained simply

**Evaluation, or eval.** A repeatable, measurable check of whether an agent's
output is correct or good enough.

**End-to-end eval.** Judging only the final output of the whole pipeline, not
any individual step inside it.

**Component-level eval.** Judging one specific stage of the pipeline in
isolation, so you know exactly where a failure originated.

**Root-cause tagging.** Labeling each failed example with which pipeline
component actually caused the failure, rather than just recording that it
failed.

**IoU.** Intersection over union, a standard segmentation metric measuring how
much a predicted mask overlaps with the true mask, from zero, no overlap, to
one, perfect overlap.

**LLM-as-judge.** Using a language model to score subjective quality that a
hard numeric threshold cannot capture cleanly.

## Two levels of evaluation

End-to-end evaluation looks only at the final output: did the pipeline
correctly flag this X-ray image as containing a void, yes or no. Simple, but it
tells you nothing about why a case failed.

Component-level evaluation scores each stage separately: did normalization
produce a sane image, did the segmentation model produce a plausible mask, did
postprocessing apply containment correctly. This is where the actual
diagnostic value lives, and it's the level I spend most of my own time at.

## Objective versus subjective evals

Some checks are objective and code-based: does the void ratio exceed a
threshold, does the mask pass a containment rule, does the output JSON parse.
Others are subjective and need an LLM-as-judge, or a human: does this mask look
like a real void to an experienced inspector. I use both, and I've learned the
hard way that skipping the subjective side just because it's harder to automate
leaves real failure modes invisible.

## The component-tagging method

This is the specific technique worth calling out on its own, and it's the one
I actually run against my own error logs. When I have a batch of failed
examples, I do not just tally "it failed." I tag which pipeline component
caused each failure, one row per failed example, one column per component. That
turns a vague sense of "the model isn't great" into a concrete, ranked list of
what to fix next.

```python
import pandas as pd

error_log = pd.DataFrame([
    {"image_id": "scan_0451", "failure_mode": "void_ratio_too_high",
     "root_cause_component": "postprocessing", "notes": "containment logic skipped"},
    {"image_id": "scan_0487", "failure_mode": "void_missed_entirely",
     "root_cause_component": "segmentation_model", "notes": "low contrast region"},
    {"image_id": "scan_0512", "failure_mode": "chip_boundary_wrong",
     "root_cause_component": "normalization", "notes": "percentile clip too aggressive"},
    {"image_id": "scan_0530", "failure_mode": "void_missed_entirely",
     "root_cause_component": "segmentation_model", "notes": "unusual solder geometry"},
    {"image_id": "scan_0561", "failure_mode": "false_positive_void",
     "root_cause_component": "confidence_estimation", "notes": "high-entropy case not flagged"},
])

component_counts = error_log["root_cause_component"].value_counts()
print(component_counts)
```

Running this on even a modest batch of failures gives me a ranked answer to
where the team should spend next sprint. If segmentation_model shows up in
forty percent of failures and normalization shows up in five percent, that's
the priority order, not a guess based on whoever complained loudest.

## Turning the tally into a component eval

Once I know segmentation_model is the biggest bucket, I build a focused,
repeatable eval just for that component, so I can measure whether a fix
actually helped, instead of eyeballing a handful of images and hoping.

```python
def component_eval_segmentation(predicted_mask, ground_truth_mask):
    """Objective, code-based component eval for the segmentation stage only,
    independent of normalization or postprocessing quality."""
    import numpy as np

    intersection = np.logical_and(predicted_mask, ground_truth_mask).sum()
    union = np.logical_or(predicted_mask, ground_truth_mask).sum()
    iou = intersection / max(union, 1)
    return {"iou": iou, "pass": iou > 0.7}
```

I run this before and after any change to the segmentation model specifically,
so the signal stays clean, not muddied by an upstream normalization issue or a
downstream postprocessing bug.

## LLM-as-judge for the subjective side

For failure modes that are genuinely hard to define with a hard threshold, for
example whether a mask looks anatomically plausible to an experienced
inspector, an LLM-as-judge call, ideally my own local vision-language model,
does a first pass at scale, with a human only reviewing the cases it flags as
uncertain.

```python
def llm_judge_plausibility(client, image_b64, mask_description):
    prompt_text = (
        "You are an experienced semiconductor X-ray inspector. Given this "
        "image and a text description of a predicted void mask, rate "
        "plausibility as plausible, borderline, or implausible, with one "
        "sentence of reasoning.\\n\\nMask description: " + mask_description
    )
    response = client.chat.completions.create(
        model="openai:gpt-4o-mini",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [
            {"type": "text", "text": prompt_text},
            {"type": "image_url", "image_url": {"url": "data:image/png;base64," + image_b64}}
        ]}]
    )
    return response.choices[0].message.content
```

## The build-analyze loop

The course frames this as a repeating loop, not a one-time audit, and that
matches how I actually work: build, run a batch, tag failures by component, fix
the highest-count component, re-run, repeat. Each cycle should shrink the error
log and shift which component tops the list. That shift is itself useful
information, it tells you the previous fix actually worked.

## Cost and latency, briefly

The course also flags benchmarking cost and latency per component as part of a
full evaluation practice, and I take that seriously too, since a component
that's accurate but ten times slower than everything else becomes my real
bottleneck once I'm running thousands of images a day. I go into this properly
in the [advanced capstone post](06-advanced-agentic-development.qmd).
